packet.description_seed: An outbreak of Ebola in DR Congo involves a rare species of the virus and is in an area affected by conflict.

what: What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

clean_source_blocks.text: An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been declared a public health emergency of international concern, by the World Health Organization (WHO). The latest outbreak is challenging because it involves a rare species of Ebola for which there is no vaccine, and the epicentre is in an area affected by conflict. The WHO has told the BBC that the outbreak may be spreading faster than originally thought. Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus. Ebola viruses normally infect animals, typically fruit bats, but outbreaks among humans can sometimes start when people eat or handle infected animals. It takes two to 21 days for symptoms to appear. They come on suddenly and start like the flu or malaria, with fever, headache and tiredness.
An outbreak of Ebola in DR Congo involves a rare species of the virus and is in an area affected by conflict.

One study showed that it killed about a third of those infected, far less than the more common Zaire (66.6%) and Sudan (48.5%) species. Initial blood tests for Ebola in the affected areas were negative as they were designed to identify the more common species of the disease. There is no approved vaccine for Bundibugyo, but experimental ones are in development. It is possible that a vaccine for the Zaire species may offer some protection. There are also no drugs that target Bundibugyo, making it harder to treat. A further complication is that the outbreak is taking place in a conflict zone, with a quarter of million people displaced from their homes and people moving across porous borders into neighbouring countries.

As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. Ebola outbreaks used to be small and contained to remote rural areas. However, urbanisation is pushing larger populations closer to these natural reservoirs of Ebola and increasing the risk of transmission. This outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which had not been seen for over a decade. Named after a district in Uganda where it was first detected, Bundibugyo has only caused two previous outbreaks - in 2007 and 2012.

[Lähde: The Guardian]
A rare strain, conflict and aid cuts make this outbreak more dangerous than ever. In the interconnected world we live in, the west can’t afford to turn away

Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

At the weekend the World Health Organization (WHO) declared an outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) a “public health emergency of international concern”. This designation is the highest alarm level the WHO has to notify its member states about a health crisis that is considered extraordinary, has multi-country risk and requires a coordinated international response. Usually, the director general, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, would convene a meeting of international health experts to discuss whether an outbreak meets the legal criteria, but for the first time in the agency’s history, he went ahead and declared it after consulting the governments of the DRC and Uganda, and analysing the data presented.

So what is happening now and why are health experts so concerned? We recently learned that there are several hundred suspected cases and 131 suspected deaths from Ebola in the eastern part of the DRC and possibly neighbouring Uganda. Ebola is one of the world’s most deadly infectious diseases, with symptoms progressing from fever and vomiting to internal bleeding and organ failure.

Most of the 16 previous outbreaks of Ebola in the DRC have been caused by the Zaire strain. For Zaire, we have a highly effective vaccine, targeted therapeutics and rapid diagnostics. Unfortunately, this latest outbreak is of the Bundibugyo strain, which does not have any medical countermeasures. Part of the reason that Ebola has been spreading for weeks undetected in communities, and into hospitals, is because rapid diagnostics for Zaire failed to identify the Bundibugyo strain. Without specific drugs, the treatment for Bundibugyo is general medical support, with death rates estimated at between 30% and 40% of those infected.

Ebola spreads through the body fluids of infected people: think saliva, blood, sweat, vaginal fluids or semen. Those most at risk are healthcare workers and family members taking care of sick patients, as well as those involved with the burial and treatment of dead bodies. Stopping the spread requires ensuring those caring for Ebola patients have adequate personal protective equipment (PPE) to protect themselves, as well as tracing contacts and ensuring they isolate before further transmission

[Lähde: Utah Public Radio]
Over the span of a few days, public health officials went from announcing a new Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo on May 15 and Uganda to declaring it an international public health emergency two days later.

By that time, the toll was notable. More than 200 people had been infected, and more than 80 had died before the disease was identified as a rare strain of Ebola, the viral hemorrhagic fever that sparked a global outbreak in 2014.

There are two critical questions about timing: When did this outbreak actually start? And why did public health officials detect it so late?

And there's another key question to consider: Has the U.S., which has traditionally been a key player in emerging outbreaks, been hampered in its response by its withdrawal from the World Health Organization?

payload.title: Kongon Ebola-epidemiaa vaikeuttaa harvinainen virusmuoto ja konfliktialue
payload.summary: WHO on julistanut Kongon demokraattisen tasavallan Ebola-epidemian kansainväliseksi kansanterveysuhaksi. Torjuntaa vaikeuttavat harvinainen Bundibugyo-virusmuoto, rokotteen puute ja levottomuudet epidemian keskusalueella.
payload.content:
Kongon demokraattisessa tasavallassa todettu Ebola-epidemia on julistettu kansainväliseksi kansanterveysuhaksi, ja sen torjuntaa pidetään poikkeuksellisen vaikeana harvinaisen virusmuodon, rokotepuutteen ja alueen konfliktitilanteen vuoksi. Maailman terveysjärjestö WHO:n mukaan epidemia voi levitä aiemmin arvioitua nopeammin.

## Harvinainen Ebola-muoto vaikeuttaa tunnistamista

Kyse on Bundibugyo-nimisestä Ebola-virusmuodosta, jota ei ole nähty yli vuosikymmeneen. Se havaittiin ensimmäisen kerran Ugandassa Bundibugyon alueella, ja sen tiedetään aiheuttaneen aiemmin vain kaksi epidemiaa, vuosina 2007 ja 2012.

Ebola on harvinainen mutta hengenvaarallinen virustauti. Ebola-virukset tartuttavat yleensä eläimiä, erityisesti hedelmälepakoita, mutta ihmisepidemiat voivat alkaa, kun ihminen syö tai käsittelee tartunnan saanutta eläintä. Oireet ilmaantuvat tavallisesti 2–21 päivän kuluessa. Alkuvaihe voi muistuttaa influenssaa tai malariaa: oireisiin kuuluu kuumetta, päänsärkyä ja väsymystä.

Taudin edetessä voi kehittyä oksentelua ja ripulia, ja vakavissa tapauksissa seurauksena voi olla elinten vajaatoiminta. Osalle sairastuneista kehittyy myös sisäistä tai ulkoista verenvuotoa. Virus leviää ihmisestä toiseen tartunnan saaneiden kehon nesteiden, kuten veren tai oksennuksen, välityksellä.

## Rokotteen puute ja konfliktit hidastavat torjuntaa

Bundibugyo-muotoon ei ole hyväksyttyä rokotetta eikä sitä vastaan kohdennettuja lääkkeitä. Kokeellisia rokotteita kehitetään, ja Zaire-virusmuotoa vastaan käytettävä rokote saattaa mahdollisesti antaa jonkinlaista suojaa, mutta varmaa ratkaisua ei ole.

Tilannetta vaikeuttaa myös se, että epidemia on konfliktialueella. Alueella on noin neljännesmiljoona kotinsa jättänyttä ihmistä, ja liikkuminen huokoisten rajojen yli naapurimaihin lisää tartuntojen jäljittämisen ja eristämisen vaikeutta.

Lisähaasteena on ollut diagnostiikka. Alueella tehdyt ensimmäiset Ebola-verikokeet olivat negatiivisia, koska testit oli suunniteltu tunnistamaan taudin yleisempiä muotoja. Yhden tutkimuksen mukaan Bundibugyo on tappanut noin kolmanneksen tartunnan saaneista, mikä on vähemmän kuin yleisemmillä Zaire- ja Sudan-virusmuodoilla, mutta tauti on silti vakava kansanterveysuhka.

Aiemmin Ebola-epidemiat jäivät usein pieniksi ja syrjäisille maaseutualueille. Kaupungistuminen on kuitenkin tuonut suurempia ihmisjoukkoja lähemmäs viruksen luonnollisia esiintymisalueita, mikä voi kasvattaa tartuntariskiä ja vaikeuttaa epidemioiden rajaamista.

Torjuntaa vaikeuttavat konfliktialue, väestön liikkuminen ja alkuvaiheen testauksen ongelmat.

One study showed that it killed about a third of those infected, far less than the more common Zaire (66.6%) and Sudan (48.5%) species. Initial blood tests for Ebola in the affected areas were negative as they were designed to identify the more common species of the disease. There is no approved vaccine for Bundibugyo, but experimental ones are in development. It is possible that a vaccine for the Zaire species may offer some protection. There are also no drugs that target Bundibugyo, making it harder to treat. A further complication is that the outbreak is taking place in a conflict zone, with a quarter of million people displaced from their homes and people moving across porous borders into neighbouring countries.

As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. Ebola outbreaks used to be small and contained to remote rural areas. However, urbanisation is pushing larger populations closer to these natural reservoirs of Ebola and increasing the risk of transmission. This outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which had not been seen for over a decade. Named after a district in Uganda where it was first detected, Bundibugyo has only caused two previous outbreaks - in 2007 and 2012.
